## TL;DR

I find Copilot most useful when the task is clear enough that I can judge its result. Start by understanding the existing code, agree on the behavior you want, and ask for a change small enough to review. Give the assistant relevant project context, keep sensitive data out of its reach, and check its work against independent expectations. More elaborate instructions, stronger models, and additional agents can help, but none replaces those basics.

In [Agents Are Easy. Products Are Still Hard.](../agents/), I wrote about the distance between a convincing prototype and something a team can maintain. I used [gridify](https://github.com/pharmaverse/gridify) as a public example. This post is the practical companion: what does that lesson look like when you open VS Code and start working?

I often work with R packages, so I will use a small R example. The package and function in the example are fictional; the decisions are ones I encounter in real software: what happens to missing values, which defaults must remain stable, and how do we know a change is correct?

## Start with the task

An assistant can produce code before I have fully decided what I want the code to do. That can be useful when exploring an idea. It can also make an unresolved decision look like progress.

I choose the level of assistance based on the task. For a familiar piece of code, an inline suggestion or a few lines written by hand may be enough. For an unfamiliar codebase, I might ask a question first. When a change involves competing requirements or compatibility, I want a plan before edits. Once the behavior is agreed, an agent can help implement and test it.

In VS Code, the available **Ask**, **Plan**, and **Agent** options depend on the session and harness. Check the selected tools and permissions rather than assuming that a request phrased as a plan cannot make changes.

One easy detail to miss: VS Code's [custom-instructions documentation](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agent-customization/custom-instructions) says those instructions are **not applied to inline suggestions** as you type. Repository guidance for chat is not a substitute for reviewing autocomplete.

## Know what is running

Copilot is more than a model. The *harness* coordinates the conversation, context, tools, and approvals. The model generates the response within that workflow.

For example, selecting a Claude model in a Copilot session does not turn the session into Claude Code. The model may be the same family, but the harness, tool access, instructions, and account policies can differ. The same distinction applies when comparing other tools.

Before starting a task in VS Code, I check the session target, selected agent, model, and permissions. Those are separate choices, and the available combinations depend on the account and organization. The [VS Code harness guide](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agents/run/agent-harnesses) is a useful reference when a feature behaves differently from what you expect.

## Keep sensitive data out of reach

Before giving an assistant access to a project, check that the account, model provider, extensions, and integrations are approved for the material involved. For examples and debugging, use synthetic fixtures and sanitized errors wherever possible. A personal subscription or an unapproved API key is not a workaround for an organization’s policy.

An instruction such as “do not read this folder” expresses intent; it does not prevent a tool from accessing that folder. `.gitignore`, editor search exclusions, and Copilot content exclusions also solve different problems.

At the time I checked, GitHub's [content-exclusion support table](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/context/content-exclusion) listed exclusions as supported for VS Code chat and inline suggestions, but **not for Edit and Agent modes**. Check the current table for your client and mode rather than assuming the same protection applies everywhere.

Look beyond the files visible in Explorer. Terminal commands, child processes, MCP servers, credentials, and network access may expose other resources. [Agent sandboxing](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agents/run/security) can restrict supported terminal processes, but its network settings need separate attention. A container or worktree alone does not ensure the controls you need: mounts, credentials, and services still need review.

I also treat material returned by tools or retrieved from the web as input, not as instructions to follow. A document can contain a prompt-injection attempt just as a repository can contain untrusted code. Limit the tools available for the task, review consequential actions, and follow your organization's incident process if sensitive data is exposed.

## Give Copilot useful project context

The most useful project instructions explain what an assistant cannot easily infer from reading one file: why an interface must stay stable, which domain rules matter, and where the team records decisions.

For the fictional R package, a short `.github/copilot-instructions.md` could look like this:

```markdown
# Project context

This package validates analysis inputs and produces aggregate summaries.
Public defaults and output fields are compatibility contracts.

# Working rules

- Read the relevant implementation and tests before editing.
- Confirm missing-value behavior and denominator definitions.
- Use synthetic fixtures; do not put input records in error messages.
- Do not add dependencies or change unrelated modules without approval.
- Run the repository's documented checks and report what actually ran.
```

I would rather maintain a file like this than a long list telling the assistant to “write clean code.” The first contains facts about the project. The second leaves the difficult decisions just as vague as before.

For guidance that applies only to part of a repository, VS Code supports scoped `.instructions.md` files. For example, `.github/instructions/r-tests.instructions.md` could contain:

```markdown
---
description: "Use when adding or changing R package tests."
applyTo: "tests/**/*.R"
---

- Follow the existing testthat conventions.
- Cover empty, all-missing, mixed, and complete inputs.
- Check expected values independently of the implementation.
```

The pattern is relative to the workspace root. Keep it narrow enough that test-specific guidance is not attached to every task.

### When a recurring task deserves a skill

If the team repeatedly asks for the same kind of work, an [Agent Skill](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agent-customization/agent-skills) can package the procedure. For example, `.github/skills/plan-change/SKILL.md` might contain:

```markdown
---
name: plan-change
description: "Plan a bounded change before editing when behavior or compatibility is unclear."
---

Read the relevant code and tests. Summarize current behavior and constraints.
Propose the change, validation, and unresolved questions. Wait for approval.
```

The folder and skill name should match. I would add a skill when it removes a recurring source of confusion, not simply because the feature exists.

Discovery depends on the selected harness. VS Code's [prompt-file documentation](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agent-customization/prompt-files), for example, describes prompt files for the Local harness; authoring one in a Copilot session does not make it runnable by the Copilot harness. Check **Chat: Open Customizations** and the documentation for your session before assuming a file is being used. Being listed, being included in a request, and being followed are different things.

## A worked example: changing missing-value behavior

Suppose an existing package has a function called `summarize_values()`. It returns a mean and the number of observed values. Its current default propagates missing values, and we want to add an option to omit them without changing that default.

Before asking for code, I would make the intended behavior explicit:

| Input | `na_rm` | Expected mean | Observed `n` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `c(2, 4, 6)` | `FALSE` | 4 | 3 |
| `c(2, NA, 6)` | `FALSE` | `NA` | 2 |
| `c(2, NA, 6)` | `TRUE` | 4 | 2 |
| `numeric(0)` | either | `NA` | 0 |
| `c(NA_real_, NA_real_)` | either | `NA` | 0 |

For this example, I also decide that `NaN` is treated as missing, infinite values are rejected, and inputs must be ordinary integer or double vectors. These are **example requirements**, not universal statistical rules. In a real package, the domain, users, and existing contract determine the right choices.

The distinction between the mean and `n` is deliberate. `n` counts observed values even when the default mean is missing. A different package might define it differently; that is precisely why it should be written down.

### First, inspect what exists

I would start with a read-only request:

> Read `summarize_values()` and its tests. Explain the current treatment of missing values, the output fields, and any compatibility constraints. Point me to the relevant definitions. Do not edit files or install anything; list questions that the code does not answer.

Then I would check the answer against the source. If the assistant says missing values are already omitted, I want to resolve that misunderstanding before it produces a patch.

### Then ask for a bounded change

Once the team agrees on the table, the implementation request can be specific:

> Add the approved `na_rm` option and regression tests. Preserve the existing default and output fields. Count observed values in both modes. Treat `NaN` as missing, reject infinite values, and return `NA` with `n = 0` for empty or all-missing input. Do not add dependencies or edit unrelated modules. Stop if the existing contract conflicts with these requirements. Report the checks you ran and their results.

An implementation for this **fictional contract** could be:

```r
summarize_values <- function(x, na_rm = FALSE) {
  if (!(typeof(x) %in% c("integer", "double")) ||
      is.object(x) || !is.null(dim(x))) {
    stop("x must be an ordinary integer or double vector.", call. = FALSE)
  }
  if (!is.logical(na_rm) || length(na_rm) != 1L || is.na(na_rm)) {
    stop("na_rm must be TRUE or FALSE.", call. = FALSE)
  }
  if (any(is.infinite(x))) {
    stop("Observed values must be finite.", call. = FALSE)
  }

  n <- sum(!is.na(x))
  value <- if (n == 0L || (!na_rm && anyNA(x))) {
    NA_real_
  } else {
    mean(x, na.rm = na_rm)
  }

  list(mean = value, n = n)
}
```

This is an illustration, not a recommendation to replace an existing package's implementation. Real code has to fit the package's public API, validation conventions, and domain requirements.

### Check the answer independently

For `c(2, NA, 6)` with omission requested, the observed values sum to 8 and there are two of them. The expected mean is 4. We know that from the requirement and a simple calculation, not from asking the implementation what answer it produced.

The following tests use `testthat` to exercise the main decisions:

```r
testthat::test_that("the default propagates missing values", {
  result <- summarize_values(c(2, NA, 6))
  testthat::expect_identical(result, list(mean = NA_real_, n = 2L))
})

testthat::test_that("explicit omission uses observed values", {
  expected <- list(mean = 4, n = 2L)
  testthat::expect_identical(summarize_values(c(2, NA, 6), TRUE), expected)
  testthat::expect_identical(summarize_values(c(2, NaN, 6), TRUE), expected)
})

testthat::test_that("no observations has a defined result", {
  for (x in list(numeric(0), c(NA_real_, NA_real_))) {
    for (na_rm in c(FALSE, TRUE)) {
      testthat::expect_identical(
        summarize_values(x, na_rm),
        list(mean = NA_real_, n = 0L)
      )
    }
  }
})

testthat::test_that("invalid options and infinite values are rejected", {
  testthat::expect_error(summarize_values(1, na_rm = NA), "na_rm")
  testthat::expect_error(summarize_values(c(1, Inf)), "finite")
})
```

These are illustrative tests, not a complete package suite. I would also check complete inputs, compatibility with existing callers, and diagnostics. A test written by the same assistant can repeat the implementation's misunderstanding, so existing regression tests and domain review still matter.

Finally, I inspect the diff. Did the assistant preserve the default? Did it change another public field, add a dependency, or modify unrelated files? I want the handover to distinguish **passed**, **failed**, and **not run**. A proposed test is not a passing test, and a targeted test is not a full package check.

## Choosing a model

Model selection matters, but it is easy to spend time debating model names when the task or context is the real problem.

For everyday work, an approved default or **Auto**, when available, is a reasonable place to start. VS Code also documents **Efficiency**, **Balance**, and **Intelligence** preferences for Auto where the service offers them; some Copilot sessions may show **Copilot Fusion** instead. Availability, model choices, and billing depend on the account and organization, so check the [current model documentation](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agent-customization/language-models).

For a routine explanation, I may not need a particular model. For an ambiguous design or a difficult failure, I may try a more capable approved model or ask for a second approach. Before switching, though, I check whether I supplied the actual error, relevant code, and constraints. A stronger model cannot infer a domain decision the team has not made.

When comparing models or products, use the same representative task and include review time and rework. A quick answer that requires an hour to untangle is not necessarily the cheaper option.

## Make the work reviewable by the team

Copilot fits inside an existing delivery process; it does not need a separate ceremony. A backlog item can still describe the outcome and acceptance criteria. A developer can use an assistant to explore or implement part of it. The team still decides whether the result meets its Definition of Done.

For a pull request, I want a short account of what changed, the decisions that matter to a reviewer, and the checks that actually ran. If something could not be tested, say so. Follow team policy on disclosing material AI assistance, and avoid pasting a confidential chat transcript when a concise summary will do.

The developer responsible for the change should be able to explain it. “The agent wrote it” does not tell a reviewer why a default changed or why an edge case is safe.

I would judge the process by outcomes such as review effort, rework, and escaped defects—not by the number of lines generated or how often someone opens Copilot. The point is to help the team deliver useful software, not to measure individual prompting activity.

## When more than one agent helps

Multiple agents are attractive because they promise parallel work. They also create coordination and review work. I start with a single agent and delegate only when there are genuinely separate questions.

Read-only investigation is a useful first step. One bounded task might locate relevant tests while another examines compatibility constraints. A separate review can then compare the integrated diff with the agreed behavior. Give each task a clear question, relevant context, and an expected result.

For a recurring review, a custom agent such as `.github/agents/reviewer.agent.md` could be:

```markdown
---
name: reviewer
description: "Review a bounded change against approved requirements without editing files."
tools: ['read', 'search']
---

Inspect the diff, relevant source, tests, and acceptance criteria.
Report correctness and compatibility findings with references.
Separate confirmed defects from questions and missing evidence.
Do not edit files or approve a merge.
```

Tool names and availability depend on the harness and extensions. Check the effective tool list in the customizations editor; the text “do not edit” is not a substitute for limiting the tools. See the [custom-agent](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agent-customization/custom-agents) and [subagent](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agents/run/subagents) documentation for the selected session.

For parallel implementation, agree on the interface and file ownership first, and integrate the results deliberately. In a larger version of the R example, one task might work on validation and another on aggregation. If the validator silently removes missing values before aggregation, both tasks could pass their own tests while the combined function breaks the default. A test through the full path is what exposes that mismatch.

Separate conversations do not necessarily mean separate files. Git worktrees can keep edits apart, but a new worktree starts from committed state; it does not automatically include uncommitted changes or ignored dependencies. It also does not isolate credentials, networks, or other resources.

There is an important VS Code-specific caveat: at the time I checked, the [Agents window documentation](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agents/run/agents-window#_choose-where-an-agent-makes-changes) said its worktree sessions use **Allow all** and do not offer manual approval prompts. Check the current behavior and your organization's policy before using that workflow. If the required controls are unavailable, work sequentially or use a separately prepared environment with appropriate permissions.

## Closing

The fastest part of AI-assisted programming is often getting something that looks plausible. The work I care about is what follows: understanding the change, checking its behavior, and making it possible for someone else to maintain.

Some tasks deserve a carefully prepared plan or a second agent. Others are quicker to solve directly. I try to choose the smallest setup that gives the team enough confidence in the result.
